Subject: Thank you for the honest feedback

Dear Minakshi,

Thank you for taking the time to reply. After my third final round, I decided to ask instead of guessing, and your answer was clear: my answers on designing large systems were hazy, and I jumped to tools before explaining the problem.

I was disappointed for a day or two, to be honest. Then I started working on it. Every Saturday I sit with a friend who plays interviewer. I draw the problem, say what could go wrong, and only then choose parts. My friend stops me whenever I get fuzzy. It is slower than I expected, but my answers are changing.

I would like to apply again in the next cycle. Thank you again.

Asif

Asif, you know how many final rounds I lost this spring? Four. I'm Kiran, and after the fourth I was ready to blame luck, or the recruiters, or my accent. Instead I did something awkward. I emailed all four hiring managers and asked, politely, "Is there one thing I could improve?"
Two replied. Both said almost the same thing: when it came to system design, I was vague. I'd draw boxes and say "this scales", but I couldn't explain how, or what would break first.
That stung. I'd thought system design was my strength. But it was clear. So for three weeks, every Sunday, my friend Rohit gave me a design problem and kept asking "and then what?" until I had real answers. My answers got shorter and more concrete.
In the next final round, they asked me to design a booking system. I got the offer, Asif.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel hearing the feedback?
qa.a: It stung Kiran, who had thought system design was a strength, but it also brought clarity.

qa.q: What made the practice with Rohit effective?
qa.a: Rohit kept asking "and then what?", forcing concrete answers about scaling and what breaks first.

qa.q: What might the hiring managers who replied have felt about Kiran's email?
qa.a: They likely respected the polite, specific request and felt it was worth answering.

grounding: It shows someone asking for feedback after several final-round rejections, learning the system design answers were vague and practising with a friend before trying again.

I share a flat with Farhan, so I saw the pattern before he did. Three companies, three final rounds, three rejections, each followed by a night of him lying on the sofa staring at the fan.
After the third, he did something I wouldn't have dared. He wrote to each interviewer and asked what he could have done better. One replied: "Strong coding, but your system design discussion stayed at a high level; we couldn't tell how you'd handle load."
He read it to me twice. He didn't say much, but the next morning he had cleared the dining table and stuck a list on the wall: payment system, chat app, ride booking. Every evening for three weeks he made me play interviewer. I'd ask, "What happens when traffic doubles?" and he'd work it out on paper until the answer was concrete.
Last Thursday he came home from a final round and didn't lie on the sofa. He made us both chai instead.
— Hrithik

qa.q: What did the interviewer's reply say?
qa.a: "Strong coding, but your system design discussion stayed at a high level; we couldn't tell how you'd handle load."

qa.q: What might Farhan have felt after each rejection?
qa.a: He seemed low and discouraged, lying on the sofa staring at the fan, though Hrithik can only see the outside.

qa.q: What else could Farhan do to keep improving?
qa.a: Ask for feedback after future interviews too, and practise with someone experienced who can push harder than a flatmate.

qa.q: How does Hrithik experience Farhan's practice?
qa.a: Hrithik plays interviewer every evening and seems glad to see Farhan come home making chai instead of lying on the sofa.
